case_info.scenario: A 43-year-old man with a progressive midfacial mass for 6 months presented at our department. Just prior to presentation, he developed epistaxis, high fever, and weight loss of 10 kg. He did not have any medical disease and denied cocaine abuse. On physical examination, an egg-sized soft mass with erythema at the edge could be observed on his nose, and the mass was covered with multiple erosions, ulcers, and exudate (Figure 1A). Laboratory examination revealed moderate anemia and elevated C-reactive protein levels. Fungal microscopic examination and culture revealed negative results, while metagenomic next-generation sequencing of the lesion showed significant positivity forPseudomonas aeruginosaand Epstein-Barr virus (EBV). Findings of computed tomography of the paranasal sinus were basically normal except for mucosal thickening. Skin biopsies were taken for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).

options.B: Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type

case_info.answer: Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type
case_info.caption: A, Clinical presentation of a destructive mass on the nose, with multiple areas of erosion, ulcers, and exudate covering the mass. B, Histological examination showed polymorphous lymphocytic infiltration in the full-thickness dermis (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: B. Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type Histopathological analysis revealed that there was polymorphous infiltrate within the full thickness of the dermis, consisting of a mixture of typical small lymphocytes and atypical lymphoid cells of varying sizes (Figure 1B). Moreover, angiodestruction and fibrinoid changes in the blood vessel wall could also be seen. Immunohistochemistry staining demonstrated increased expression of CD2, CD56, and cytoplasmic CD3 in atypical cells (Figure 2). In addition, in situ hybridization revealed positivity for EBV-encoded small nuclear RNA in the dermis. The diagnosis of extranodal natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (ENKL-NT) was validated based on histological features, laboratory findings, and clinical characteristics. Following radiotherapy, the patient died with severe cachexia. ENKL-NT is a malignant EBV-associated lymphoma characterized by rapid progression and a poor prognosis, and it occurs more commonly in Asia and Latin America than in other regions.1Clinically, it presents as a necrotizing mass involving the nose, sinuses, or palate accompanied by localized symptoms, such as nasal obstruction and epistaxis. Common systemic symptoms are fever and weight loss.2From a histological perspective, ENKL-NT is commonly distinguished by the presence of local angioinvasion and angiodestruction, leading to the gradual development of necrotic ulceration. The neoplastic cells are intermediate to large in size and display positivity for the surface markers CD2 and CD56 as well as for the cytoplasmic expression of CD3ε. However, these cells lack surface expression of CD3.2 The diagnosis of ENKL-NT may be challenging clinically due to its similarity to other midline destructive lesions, which mainly include rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LYG). Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis and often occurs in immunocompromised patients and those with diabetes. Ulceration covered by black eschar on the midfacial region, periorbital swelling, and sinusitis are its 3 hallmarks.3Pathologically, the presence of characteristic hyphae provides a presumptive diagnosis that should prompt further evaluation. Widespread infiltration of normal lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells can also be observed.4Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that can involve the respiratory tract and kidneys, causing coughing, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and kidney insufficiency in addition to midline destructive lesions.5Noncaseating granulomas and leukocytoclastic vasculitis are the typical histological findings.6Similar in histology to ENKL-NT, LYG is another EBV-positive tumor that may appear at extranodal sites. However, in LYG, EBV-positive tumor cells originate from B cells and therefore express pan–B-cell markers, such as CD20, instead of markers typical of NK or T cells.7 Unfortunately, to our knowledge, no standard treatment for ENKL-NT has been determined. Radiation therapy is a fundamental part of first-line treatment for patients with localized ENKL-NT, and concurrent or sequential chemotherapy combinations may be more effective than single-agent regimens.8Chemotherapy containing L-asparaginase is an essential component of recommended treatments for advanced ENKL-NT.8A poor prognosis was significantly associated with non–nasal-type disease, involvement of distant lymph nodes, advanced disease, and age older than 60 years.9Early diagnosis and treatment of ENKL-NT can improve overall survival, prevent disfiguration, and improve patient quality of life.

   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.caption: A, Clinical presentation of a destructive mass on the nose, with multiple areas of erosion, ulcers, and exudate covering the mass. B, Histological examination showed polymorphous lymphocytic infiltration in the full-thickness dermis (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: B. Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type Histopathological analysis revealed that there was polymorphous infiltrate within the full thickness of the dermis, consisting of a mixture of typical small lymphocytes and atypical lymphoid cells of varying sizes (Figure 1B). Moreover, angiodestruction and fibrinoid changes in the blood vessel wall could also be seen. Immunohistochemistry staining demonstrated increased expression of CD2, CD56, and cytoplasmic CD3 in atypical cells (Figure 2). In addition, in situ hybridization revealed positivity for EBV-encoded small nuclear RNA in the dermis. The diagnosis of extranodal natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (ENKL-NT) was validated based on histological features, laboratory findings, and clinical characteristics. Following radiotherapy, the patient died with severe cachexia. ENKL-NT is a malignant EBV-associated lymphoma characterized by rapid progression and a poor prognosis, and it occurs more commonly in Asia and Latin America than in other regions.1Clinically, it presents as a necrotizing mass involving the nose, sinuses, or palate accompanied by localized symptoms, such as nasal obstruction and epistaxis. Common systemic symptoms are fever and weight loss.2From a histological perspective, ENKL-NT is commonly distinguished by the presence of local angioinvasion and angiodestruction, leading to the gradual development of necrotic ulceration. The neoplastic cells are intermediate to large in size and display positivity for the surface markers CD2 and CD56 as well as for the cytoplasmic expression of CD3ε. However, these cells lack surface expression of CD3.2 The diagnosis of ENKL-NT may be challenging clinically due to its similarity to other midline destructive lesions, which mainly include rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LYG). Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis and often occurs in immunocompromised patients and those with diabetes. Ulceration covered by black eschar on the midfacial region, periorbital swelling, and sinusitis are its 3 hallmarks.3Pathologically, the presence of characteristic hyphae provides a presumptive diagnosis that should prompt further evaluation. Widespread infiltration of normal lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells can also be observed.4Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that can involve the respiratory tract and kidneys, causing coughing, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and kidney insufficiency in addition to midline destructive lesions.5Noncaseating granulomas and leukocytoclastic vasculitis are the typical histological findings.6Similar in histology to ENKL-NT, LYG is another EBV-positive tumor that may appear at extranodal sites. However, in LYG, EBV-positive tumor cells originate from B cells and therefore express pan–B-cell markers, such as CD20, instead of markers typical of NK or T cells.7 Unfortunately, to our knowledge, no standard treatment for ENKL-NT has been determined. Radiation therapy is a fundamental part of first-line treatment for patients with localized ENKL-NT, and concurrent or sequential chemotherapy combinations may be more effective than single-agent regimens.8Chemotherapy containing L-asparaginase is an essential component of recommended treatments for advanced ENKL-NT.8A poor prognosis was significantly associated with non–nasal-type disease, involvement of distant lymph nodes, advanced disease, and age older than 60 years.9Early diagnosis and treatment of ENKL-NT can improve overall survival, prevent disfiguration, and improve patient quality of life.

case_info.explanation: B. Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type Histopathological analysis revealed that there was polymorphous infiltrate within the full thickness of the dermis, consisting of a mixture of typical small lymphocytes and atypical lymphoid cells of varying sizes (Figure 1B). Moreover, angiodestruction and fibrinoid changes in the blood vessel wall could also be seen. Immunohistochemistry staining demonstrated increased expression of CD2, CD56, and cytoplasmic CD3 in atypical cells (Figure 2). In addition, in situ hybridization revealed positivity for EBV-encoded small nuclear RNA in the dermis. The diagnosis of extranodal natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (ENKL-NT) was validated based on histological features, laboratory findings, and clinical characteristics. Following radiotherapy, the patient died with severe cachexia. ENKL-NT is a malignant EBV-associated lymphoma characterized by rapid progression and a poor prognosis, and it occurs more commonly in Asia and Latin America than in other regions.1Clinically, it presents as a necrotizing mass involving the nose, sinuses, or palate accompanied by localized symptoms, such as nasal obstruction and epistaxis. Common systemic symptoms are fever and weight loss.2From a histological perspective, ENKL-NT is commonly distinguished by the presence of local angioinvasion and angiodestruction, leading to the gradual development of necrotic ulceration. The neoplastic cells are intermediate to large in size and display positivity for the surface markers CD2 and CD56 as well as for the cytoplasmic expression of CD3ε. However, these cells lack surface expression of CD3.2 The diagnosis of ENKL-NT may be challenging clinically due to its similarity to other midline destructive lesions, which mainly include rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LYG). Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis and often occurs in immunocompromised patients and those with diabetes. Ulceration covered by black eschar on the midfacial region, periorbital swelling, and sinusitis are its 3 hallmarks.3Pathologically, the presence of characteristic hyphae provides a presumptive diagnosis that should prompt further evaluation. Widespread infiltration of normal lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells can also be observed.4Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that can involve the respiratory tract and kidneys, causing coughing, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and kidney insufficiency in addition to midline destructive lesions.5Noncaseating granulomas and leukocytoclastic vasculitis are the typical histological findings.6Similar in histology to ENKL-NT, LYG is another EBV-positive tumor that may appear at extranodal sites. However, in LYG, EBV-positive tumor cells originate from B cells and therefore express pan–B-cell markers, such as CD20, instead of markers typical of NK or T cells.7 Unfortunately, to our knowledge, no standard treatment for ENKL-NT has been determined. Radiation therapy is a fundamental part of first-line treatment for patients with localized ENKL-NT, and concurrent or sequential chemotherapy combinations may be more effective than single-agent regimens.8Chemotherapy containing L-asparaginase is an essential component of recommended treatments for advanced ENKL-NT.8A poor prognosis was significantly associated with non–nasal-type disease, involvement of distant lymph nodes, advanced disease, and age older than 60 years.9Early diagnosis and treatment of ENKL-NT can improve overall survival, prevent disfiguration, and improve patient quality of life.

case_info.answer: Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type
case_info.caption: A, Clinical presentation of a destructive mass on the nose, with multiple areas of erosion, ulcers, and exudate covering the mass. B, Histological examination showed polymorphous lymphocytic infiltration in the full-thickness dermis (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: B. Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type Histopathological analysis revealed that there was polymorphous infiltrate within the full thickness of the dermis, consisting of a mixture of typical small lymphocytes and atypical lymphoid cells of varying sizes (Figure 1B). Moreover, angiodestruction and fibrinoid changes in the blood vessel wall could also be seen. Immunohistochemistry staining demonstrated increased expression of CD2, CD56, and cytoplasmic CD3 in atypical cells (Figure 2). In addition, in situ hybridization revealed positivity for EBV-encoded small nuclear RNA in the dermis. The diagnosis of extranodal natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (ENKL-NT) was validated based on histological features, laboratory findings, and clinical characteristics. Following radiotherapy, the patient died with severe cachexia. ENKL-NT is a malignant EBV-associated lymphoma characterized by rapid progression and a poor prognosis, and it occurs more commonly in Asia and Latin America than in other regions.1Clinically, it presents as a necrotizing mass involving the nose, sinuses, or palate accompanied by localized symptoms, such as nasal obstruction and epistaxis. Common systemic symptoms are fever and weight loss.2From a histological perspective, ENKL-NT is commonly distinguished by the presence of local angioinvasion and angiodestruction, leading to the gradual development of necrotic ulceration. The neoplastic cells are intermediate to large in size and display positivity for the surface markers CD2 and CD56 as well as for the cytoplasmic expression of CD3ε. However, these cells lack surface expression of CD3.2 The diagnosis of ENKL-NT may be challenging clinically due to its similarity to other midline destructive lesions, which mainly include rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LYG). Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis and often occurs in immunocompromised patients and those with diabetes. Ulceration covered by black eschar on the midfacial region, periorbital swelling, and sinusitis are its 3 hallmarks.3Pathologically, the presence of characteristic hyphae provides a presumptive diagnosis that should prompt further evaluation. Widespread infiltration of normal lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells can also be observed.4Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that can involve the respiratory tract and kidneys, causing coughing, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and kidney insufficiency in addition to midline destructive lesions.5Noncaseating granulomas and leukocytoclastic vasculitis are the typical histological findings.6Similar in histology to ENKL-NT, LYG is another EBV-positive tumor that may appear at extranodal sites. However, in LYG, EBV-positive tumor cells originate from B cells and therefore express pan–B-cell markers, such as CD20, instead of markers typical of NK or T cells.7 Unfortunately, to our knowledge, no standard treatment for ENKL-NT has been determined. Radiation therapy is a fundamental part of first-line treatment for patients with localized ENKL-NT, and concurrent or sequential chemotherapy combinations may be more effective than single-agent regimens.8Chemotherapy containing L-asparaginase is an essential component of recommended treatments for advanced ENKL-NT.8A poor prognosis was significantly associated with non–nasal-type disease, involvement of distant lymph nodes, advanced disease, and age older than 60 years.9Early diagnosis and treatment of ENKL-NT can improve overall survival, prevent disfiguration, and improve patient quality of life.

case_info.answer: Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type
case_info.caption: A, Clinical presentation of a destructive mass on the nose, with multiple areas of erosion, ulcers, and exudate covering the mass. B, Histological examination showed polymorphous lymphocytic infiltration in the full-thickness dermis (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: B. Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type Histopathological analysis revealed that there was polymorphous infiltrate within the full thickness of the dermis, consisting of a mixture of typical small lymphocytes and atypical lymphoid cells of varying sizes (Figure 1B). Moreover, angiodestruction and fibrinoid changes in the blood vessel wall could also be seen. Immunohistochemistry staining demonstrated increased expression of CD2, CD56, and cytoplasmic CD3 in atypical cells (Figure 2). In addition, in situ hybridization revealed positivity for EBV-encoded small nuclear RNA in the dermis. The diagnosis of extranodal natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (ENKL-NT) was validated based on histological features, laboratory findings, and clinical characteristics. Following radiotherapy, the patient died with severe cachexia. ENKL-NT is a malignant EBV-associated lymphoma characterized by rapid progression and a poor prognosis, and it occurs more commonly in Asia and Latin America than in other regions.1Clinically, it presents as a necrotizing mass involving the nose, sinuses, or palate accompanied by localized symptoms, such as nasal obstruction and epistaxis. Common systemic symptoms are fever and weight loss.2From a histological perspective, ENKL-NT is commonly distinguished by the presence of local angioinvasion and angiodestruction, leading to the gradual development of necrotic ulceration. The neoplastic cells are intermediate to large in size and display positivity for the surface markers CD2 and CD56 as well as for the cytoplasmic expression of CD3ε. However, these cells lack surface expression of CD3.2 The diagnosis of ENKL-NT may be challenging clinically due to its similarity to other midline destructive lesions, which mainly include rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LYG). Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis and often occurs in immunocompromised patients and those with diabetes. Ulceration covered by black eschar on the midfacial region, periorbital swelling, and sinusitis are its 3 hallmarks.3Pathologically, the presence of characteristic hyphae provides a presumptive diagnosis that should prompt further evaluation. Widespread infiltration of normal lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells can also be observed.4Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that can involve the respiratory tract and kidneys, causing coughing, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and kidney insufficiency in addition to midline destructive lesions.5Noncaseating granulomas and leukocytoclastic vasculitis are the typical histological findings.6Similar in histology to ENKL-NT, LYG is another EBV-positive tumor that may appear at extranodal sites. However, in LYG, EBV-positive tumor cells originate from B cells and therefore express pan–B-cell markers, such as CD20, instead of markers typical of NK or T cells.7 Unfortunately, to our knowledge, no standard treatment for ENKL-NT has been determined. Radiation therapy is a fundamental part of first-line treatment for patients with localized ENKL-NT, and concurrent or sequential chemotherapy combinations may be more effective than single-agent regimens.8Chemotherapy containing L-asparaginase is an essential component of recommended treatments for advanced ENKL-NT.8A poor prognosis was significantly associated with non–nasal-type disease, involvement of distant lymph nodes, advanced disease, and age older than 60 years.9Early diagnosis and treatment of ENKL-NT can improve overall survival, prevent disfiguration, and improve patient quality of life.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.caption: A, Clinical presentation of a destructive mass on the nose, with multiple areas of erosion, ulcers, and exudate covering the mass. case_info.explanation: B. Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type Histopathological analysis revealed that there was polymorphous infiltrate within the full thickness of the dermis, consisting of a mixture of typical small lymphocytes and atypical lymphoid cells of varying sizes (Figure 1B). Moreover, angiodestruction and fibrinoid changes in the blood vessel wall could also be seen. Immunohistochemistry staining demonstrated increased expression of CD2, CD56, and cytoplasmic CD3 in atypical cells (Figure 2). In addition, in situ hybridization revealed positivity for EBV-encoded small nuclear RNA in the dermis. The diagnosis of extranodal natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (ENKL-NT) was validated based on histological features, laboratory findings, and clinical characteristics. Following radiotherapy, the patient died with severe cachexia. ENKL-NT is a malignant EBV-associated lymphoma characterized by rapid progression and a poor prognosis, and it occurs more commonly in Asia and Latin America than in other regions.1Clinically, it presents as a necrotizing mass involving the nose, sinuses, or palate accompanied by localized symptoms, such as nasal obstruction and epistaxis. Common systemic symptoms are fever and weight loss.2From a histological perspective, ENKL-NT is commonly distinguished by the presence of local angioinvasion and angiodestruction, leading to the gradual development of necrotic ulceration. The neoplastic cells are intermediate to large in size and display positivity for the surface markers CD2 and CD56 as well as for the cytoplasmic expression of CD3ε. However, these cells lack surface expression of CD3.2 The diagnosis of ENKL-NT may be challenging clinically due to its similarity to other midline destructive lesions, which mainly include rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LYG). Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis and often occurs in immunocompromised patients and those with diabetes. Ulceration covered by black eschar on the midfacial region, periorbital swelling, and sinusitis are its 3 hallmarks.3Pathologically, the presence of characteristic hyphae provides a presumptive diagnosis that should prompt further evaluation. Widespread infiltration of normal lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells can also be observed.4Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that can involve the respiratory tract and kidneys, causing coughing, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and kidney insufficiency in addition to midline destructive lesions.5Noncaseating granulomas and leukocytoclastic vasculitis are the typical histological findings.6Similar in histology to ENKL-NT, LYG is another EBV-positive tumor that may appear at extranodal sites. However, in LYG, EBV-positive tumor cells originate from B cells and therefore express pan–B-cell markers, such as CD20, instead of markers typical of NK or T cells.7 Unfortunately, to our knowledge, no standard treatment for ENKL-NT has been determined. Radiation therapy is a fundamental part of first-line treatment for patients with localized ENKL-NT, and concurrent or sequential chemotherapy combinations may be more effective than single-agent regimens.8Chemotherapy containing L-asparaginase is an essential component of recommended treatments for advanced ENKL-NT.8A poor prognosis was significantly associated with non–nasal-type disease, involvement of distant lymph nodes, advanced disease, and age older than 60 years.9Early diagnosis and treatment of ENKL-NT can improve overall survival, prevent disfiguration, and improve patient quality of life.

case_info.answer: Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type
case_info.caption: A, Clinical presentation of a destructive mass on the nose, with multiple areas of erosion, ulcers, and exudate covering the mass. B, Histological examination showed polymorphous lymphocytic infiltration in the full-thickness dermis (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: B. Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type Histopathological analysis revealed that there was polymorphous infiltrate within the full thickness of the dermis, consisting of a mixture of typical small lymphocytes and atypical lymphoid cells of varying sizes (Figure 1B). Moreover, angiodestruction and fibrinoid changes in the blood vessel wall could also be seen. Immunohistochemistry staining demonstrated increased expression of CD2, CD56, and cytoplasmic CD3 in atypical cells (Figure 2). In addition, in situ hybridization revealed positivity for EBV-encoded small nuclear RNA in the dermis. The diagnosis of extranodal natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (ENKL-NT) was validated based on histological features, laboratory findings, and clinical characteristics. Following radiotherapy, the patient died with severe cachexia. ENKL-NT is a malignant EBV-associated lymphoma characterized by rapid progression and a poor prognosis, and it occurs more commonly in Asia and Latin America than in other regions.1Clinically, it presents as a necrotizing mass involving the nose, sinuses, or palate accompanied by localized symptoms, such as nasal obstruction and epistaxis. Common systemic symptoms are fever and weight loss.2From a histological perspective, ENKL-NT is commonly distinguished by the presence of local angioinvasion and angiodestruction, leading to the gradual development of necrotic ulceration. The neoplastic cells are intermediate to large in size and display positivity for the surface markers CD2 and CD56 as well as for the cytoplasmic expression of CD3ε. However, these cells lack surface expression of CD3.2 The diagnosis of ENKL-NT may be challenging clinically due to its similarity to other midline destructive lesions, which mainly include rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LYG). Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis and often occurs in immunocompromised patients and those with diabetes. Ulceration covered by black eschar on the midfacial region, periorbital swelling, and sinusitis are its 3 hallmarks.3Pathologically, the presence of characteristic hyphae provides a presumptive diagnosis that should prompt further evaluation. Widespread infiltration of normal lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells can also be observed.4Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that can involve the respiratory tract and kidneys, causing coughing, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and kidney insufficiency in addition to midline destructive lesions.5Noncaseating granulomas and leukocytoclastic vasculitis are the typical histological findings.6Similar in histology to ENKL-NT, LYG is another EBV-positive tumor that may appear at extranodal sites. However, in LYG, EBV-positive tumor cells originate from B cells and therefore express pan–B-cell markers, such as CD20, instead of markers typical of NK or T cells.7 Unfortunately, to our knowledge, no standard treatment for ENKL-NT has been determined. Radiation therapy is a fundamental part of first-line treatment for patients with localized ENKL-NT, and concurrent or sequential chemotherapy combinations may be more effective than single-agent regimens.8Chemotherapy containing L-asparaginase is an essential component of recommended treatments for advanced ENKL-NT.8A poor prognosis was significantly associated with non–nasal-type disease, involvement of distant lymph nodes, advanced disease, and age older than 60 years.9Early diagnosis and treatment of ENKL-NT can improve overall survival, prevent disfiguration, and improve patient quality of life.

case_info.answer: Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type
case_info.caption: A, Clinical presentation of a destructive mass on the nose, with multiple areas of erosion, ulcers, and exudate covering the mass. B, Histological examination showed polymorphous lymphocytic infiltration in the full-thickness dermis (hematoxylin-eosin, original magnification ×100).
case_info.explanation: B. Extranodal natural killer/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type Histopathological analysis revealed that there was polymorphous infiltrate within the full thickness of the dermis, consisting of a mixture of typical small lymphocytes and atypical lymphoid cells of varying sizes (Figure 1B). Moreover, angiodestruction and fibrinoid changes in the blood vessel wall could also be seen. Immunohistochemistry staining demonstrated increased expression of CD2, CD56, and cytoplasmic CD3 in atypical cells (Figure 2). In addition, in situ hybridization revealed positivity for EBV-encoded small nuclear RNA in the dermis. The diagnosis of extranodal natural killer (NK)/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (ENKL-NT) was validated based on histological features, laboratory findings, and clinical characteristics. Following radiotherapy, the patient died with severe cachexia. ENKL-NT is a malignant EBV-associated lymphoma characterized by rapid progression and a poor prognosis, and it occurs more commonly in Asia and Latin America than in other regions.1Clinically, it presents as a necrotizing mass involving the nose, sinuses, or palate accompanied by localized symptoms, such as nasal obstruction and epistaxis. Common systemic symptoms are fever and weight loss.2From a histological perspective, ENKL-NT is commonly distinguished by the presence of local angioinvasion and angiodestruction, leading to the gradual development of necrotic ulceration. The neoplastic cells are intermediate to large in size and display positivity for the surface markers CD2 and CD56 as well as for the cytoplasmic expression of CD3ε. However, these cells lack surface expression of CD3.2 The diagnosis of ENKL-NT may be challenging clinically due to its similarity to other midline destructive lesions, which mainly include rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, and lymphomatoid granulomatosis (LYG). Rhino-orbital-cerebral mucormycosis is the most common clinical presentation of mucormycosis and often occurs in immunocompromised patients and those with diabetes. Ulceration covered by black eschar on the midfacial region, periorbital swelling, and sinusitis are its 3 hallmarks.3Pathologically, the presence of characteristic hyphae provides a presumptive diagnosis that should prompt further evaluation. Widespread infiltration of normal lymphocytes and other inflammatory cells can also be observed.4Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a necrotizing vasculitis that can involve the respiratory tract and kidneys, causing coughing, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and kidney insufficiency in addition to midline destructive lesions.5Noncaseating granulomas and leukocytoclastic vasculitis are the typical histological findings.6Similar in histology to ENKL-NT, LYG is another EBV-positive tumor that may appear at extranodal sites. However, in LYG, EBV-positive tumor cells originate from B cells and therefore express pan–B-cell markers, such as CD20, instead of markers typical of NK or T cells.7 Unfortunately, to our knowledge, no standard treatment for ENKL-NT has been determined. Radiation therapy is a fundamental part of first-line treatment for patients with localized ENKL-NT, and concurrent or sequential chemotherapy combinations may be more effective than single-agent regimens.8Chemotherapy containing L-asparaginase is an essential component of recommended treatments for advanced ENKL-NT.8A poor prognosis was significantly associated with non–nasal-type disease, involvement of distant lymph nodes, advanced disease, and age older than 60 years.9Early diagnosis and treatment of ENKL-NT can improve overall survival, prevent disfiguration, and improve patient quality of life.

Findings of computed tomography of the paranasal sinus were basically normal except for mucosal thickening. Skin biopsies were taken for histopathological examination (Figure 1B).
